task_description:
Welcome, and thank you for taking part in the WMT26 syntactic test suite evaluation!

You will be shown a source sentence together with one or more machine translations of it into Icelandic, along with a syntactic category and specific instructions for that category. You will never be told which system produced a translation, and you should not try to guess. The order of the translations is randomised.

For every translation, please answer three questions:

1. Construction acceptability — Is the translation of the construction described above acceptable? Judge ONLY according to the category instructions shown above the sentence. Choose "Acceptable" if the construction described in the instructions is handled correctly, and "Unacceptable" if it is not. Ignore other errors for this question.

2. Meaning preserved — judge whether the translation preserves the meaning of the source sentence. Choose "True" if a reader of the translation would come away with the same information as a reader of the source, and "False" if important meaning is missing, added or changed.

3. Translation acceptability — Not taking into account the construction acceptability, are other parts of the translation acceptable, such as vocabulary selection, morphology or other syntactic structures?

The questions are independent: for example, a translation can render the construction acceptably but distort the meaning, and vice versa.

You can also leave an optional comment on any translation — use it for anything you want to note about the translation or your judgements.

Answer all questions for every translation on the page, then press "Submit and next sentence". If new translations of a sentence you have already judged are added later, they will appear as new questions, with your earlier evaluations of that sentence shown (read-only) below.

Practical notes:
- Your progress is saved after every sentence; you can stop and continue later at any time.
- Work at your own pace and trust your intuition as a fluent speaker.

sentences.category_instructions:
Pseudo-coordination refers to any construction with the appearance of coordination in form despite subordinative (or otherwise non-coordinative) properties. (1) exhibits verbal pseudo-coordination with "try and" (followed by a verb phrase), with a similar or the same meaning as "try to".

(1) I'm gonna try and help them.

The Icelandic translation in (2) does not contain pseudo-coordination; rather, "reyna" ‘try’, which is not compatible with pseudo-coordination in Icelandic, selects an infinitival clause with the infinitival marker "að" ‘to’.

(2) Ég ætla að reyna að hjálpa þeim.

sentences.category_instructions:
A parasitic gap is dependent on the existence of another gap. The first gap in the following is the “real” or “true gap” (rg), linked with the moved wh-phrase. The second gap is the parasitic one (pg).

(1) Which books has John burnt __(rg) without reading __(pg)?

If the wh-phrase is in situ (does not move), a parasitic gap is not licensed as shown in the echo question in (2) (the asterisk denotes ungrammaticality).

(2) *John has burnt which books, without reading __(pg)?

While parasitic gaps are found in English, they have been claimed to be never fully acceptable in Icelandic. In the translation of (1), see (3), we have added a pronoun "þær" (referring to "bækur" 'books') so there is no parasitic gap in the example.

(3) Hvaða bækur hefur Jón brennt __(rg) án þess að lesa þær?

sentences.category_instructions:
In tough movement as in (1)–(2), the adjective combines with two elements: an infinitival clause containing a gap and a subject DP that is semantically interpreted in the gap position.

(1) My pets are not easy to forget __.
(2) Which pets are not easy to forget __?

In a corresponding expletive construction, the adjective takes an infinitival clause as its argument and the matrix subject position is filled with an expletive.

(3) It is not easy to forget my pets.

Some speakers of Icelandic find the tough construction as in (4)–(5) unacceptable and prefer, e.g., the structures in (6)–(7).

(4) Gæludýrin mín eru ekki auðveld að gleyma.
(5) Hvaða gæludýr eru ekki auðveld að gleyma?

(6) Það er ekki auðvelt að gleyma gæludýrunum mínum.
(7) Hvaða gæludýrum er ekki auðvelt að gleyma?

Note that "gleyma" ‘forget’ takes a dative-case object in Icelandic. In the tough construction in (4)–(5) , dative case is not preserved and instead ‘my pets’/‘which pets’ is in the nominative case in subject position, triggering plural on the finite verb and agreement in case, number and gender on the adjective. In the expletive construction in (6), however, as well as in (7), dative case on the object is preserved and the finite verb and the adjective do not agree with ‘my pets’/‘which pets’.

sentences.category_instructions:
In tough movement as in (1)–(2), the adjective combines with two elements: an infinitival clause containing a gap and a subject DP that is semantically interpreted in the gap position.

(1) My pets are not easy to forget __.
(2) Which pets are not easy to forget __?

In a corresponding expletive construction, the adjective takes an infinitival clause as its argument and the matrix subject position is filled with an expletive.

(3) It is not easy to forget my pets.

Some speakers of Icelandic find the tough construction as in (4)–(5) unacceptable and prefer, e.g., the structures in (6)–(7).

(4) Gæludýrin mín eru ekki auðveld að gleyma.

(6) Það er ekki auðvelt að gleyma gæludýrunum mínum.
(7) Hvaða gæludýrum er ekki auðvelt að gleyma?

In the tough construction in (4)–(5) , dative case is not preserved and instead ‘my pets’/‘which pets’ is in the nominative case in subject position, triggering plural on the finite verb and agreement in case, number and gender on the adjective. Pseudo-coordination refers to any construction with the appearance of coordination in form despite subordinative (or otherwise non-coordinative) properties. (1) exhibits verbal pseudo-coordination with "try and" (followed by a verb phrase), with a similar or the same meaning as "try to".

(2) Ég ætla að reyna að hjálpa þeim.

sentences.category_instructions:
There are various modal verbs in both English and Icelandic. Some English modal verbs might have straightforward Icelandic translations whereas some other modal verbs, like English "must", can have different Icelandic translations, depending on the context – must can be deontic, epistemic, etc. "Must" in (1) has a deontic reading, whereas it has an epistemic reading in (2). Even though the two uses have the same form in English, they have two different translations in Icelandic, see (3)–(4).

(1) You must leave.
(2) You must have left early.

(3) Þú verður að fara.
(4) Þú hlýtur að hafa farið snemma.

Pseudo-coordination refers to any construction with the appearance of coordination in form despite subordinative (or otherwise non-coordinative) properties. (1) exhibits verbal pseudo-coordination with "try and" (followed by a verb phrase), with a similar or the same meaning as "try to".

(1) I'm gonna try and help them.

The Icelandic translation in (2) does not contain pseudo-coordination; rather, "reyna" ‘try’, which is not compatible with pseudo-coordination in Icelandic, selects an infinitival clause with the infinitival marker "að" ‘to’.

(2) Ég ætla að reyna að hjálpa þeim.

sentences.category_instructions:
Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

sentences.category_instructions:
Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

(1) María shook her head.

In the translation of (1), see (2), a pronominal possessor is not used (which would be an equivalent of “her”), so the literal meaning of the Icelandic translation is ‘María shook the head’.

(2) María hristi höfuðið.

sentences.category_instructions:
English pseudo-passives involve the passive together with a stranded preposition. What corresponds to the direct object of the preposition is in subject position and triggers verb agreement like regular subjects in English do.

(1) The players were screamed at.
(2) Which players were screamed at?

Icelandic allows stranded prepositions where the object of the preposition is topicalized but does not move to subject position. In the translation of the sentence in (1), see (3), the noun phrase ‘the players’ does not move at all and stays within the prepositional phrase. We show movement in the two translations of (2): In (4) the whole prepositional phrase, containing ‘which players’ is topicalized whereas only the wh-phrase moves in (5). Note that this noun phrase is topicalized and does not move to subject position in (5) (we do not go further into that here but it should be noted that the noun phrase is not in the nominative case but preserves accusative case from the preposition).

(3) Það var öskrað á leikmennina.
(4) Á hvaða leikmenn var öskrað?
(5) Hvaða leikmenn var öskrað á?

sentences.category_instructions:
Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

sentences.category_instructions:
English pseudo-passives involve the passive together with a stranded preposition. What corresponds to the direct object of the preposition is in subject position and triggers verb agreement like regular subjects in English do.

(1) The players were screamed at.
(2) Which players were screamed at?

Icelandic allows stranded prepositions where the object of the preposition is topicalized but does not move to subject position. In the translation of the sentence in (1), see (3), the noun phrase ‘the players’ does not move at all and stays within the prepositional phrase. We show movement in the two translations of (2): In (4) the whole prepositional phrase, containing ‘which players’ is topicalized whereas only the wh-phrase moves in (5). Note that this noun phrase is topicalized and does not move to subject position in (5) (we do not go further into that here but it should be noted that the noun phrase is not in the nominative case but preserves accusative case from the preposition).

(3) Það var öskrað á leikmennina.
(4) Á hvaða leikmenn var öskrað?
(5) Hvaða leikmenn var öskrað á?

(1) I'm gonna try and help them.

sentences.category_instructions:
Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

sentences.category_instructions:
Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

sentences.category_instructions:
Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

(2) He boiled her an egg.

Icelandic has a wide range of dative-case use. Indirect objects are frequently found in the dative case, as in "Jón gaf mér þessa bók" ‘John gave me this book’. In that example, "mér" ‘me’ is what is sometimes classified as a low applicative. Nonetheless, Icelandic is more restricted with respect to various applicative arguments, such that for various verbs, indirect objects are not possible unless they are reflexive. Let us look at two English examples with an applied indirect object, one of which contains a reflexive indirect object, see (1), and one of which contains a non-reflexive indirect object, see (2).

(1) He boiled himself an egg.
(2) He boiled her an egg.

The translation of (1), see (3), contains an applied reflexive dative sér (an indirect object) whereas the applied non-reflexive indirect object of (2) is translated within a prepositional phrase in (4) and (5).

(3) Hann sauð sér egg.
(4) Hann sauð egg handa henni.
(5) Hann sauð egg fyrir hana.

English has both bare relative clauses, as in (1), and reduced relative clauses, as in (2), both of which lack a relative complementizer or a relative pronoun.

A translation of both examples therefore contains a relative complementizer "sem" ‘who, that’, see (3)–(4).
